1.note: The author is speaking as if the **adversary** had actually **stood up**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the adversary took action]

The Hebrew word “satan” means “adversary.” The Old Testament uses the word in that specific sense in several places, for example, 1 Kings 11:14, “Yahweh raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite.” In the book of Job, there is a character called “the satan” or “the adversary.” This seems to be a created angelic being who opposes righteous people and accuses them before God of having wrong motives. Many interpreters of the book of Job identify this character with Satan, the devil, and many interpreters believe that the author is describing that same figure here. The UST uses a general expression. You can decide how to translate this term in your own translation.

2.note: Here and in verse 5, the term **people** means “soldiers.” Alternate translation: [the soldiers] or [his army]

2.q: לְכ֗וּ סִפְרוּ֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִ⁠בְּאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע וְ⁠עַד־דָּ֑ן וְ⁠הָבִ֣יאוּ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠אֵדְעָ֖ה אֶת־מִסְפָּרָֽ⁠ם
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [That I may know their number, go, count Israel from Beersheba and to Dan, and bring to me]

The author is using the name **Israel** to represent that man’s descendants and, in this context, specifically his male descendants who were able to fight in wars. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelite men who are able to serve as soldiers]

David is referring to all of the Israelite territory by naming two extremes, **Dan** (a city in the far north) and **Beersheba** (a city in the far south). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the entire territory of Israel]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and bring a report to me]

3.note: Joab is using **like them** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as many as they already are.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a hundred times more than there already are]

In this context, the number **a hundred** is a round, symbolic number that represents “very many.” Your language may have a number of its own that it uses with that meaning. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [many times more than there already are]

Joab is using the question form to indicate that what he describes is certainly true. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [certainly all of them are servants to my lord!]

3.q: לַ⁠אדֹנִ֖⁠י לַ⁠עֲבָדִ֑ים לָ֣⁠מָּה יְבַקֵּ֥שׁ זֹאת֙ אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י
3.note: Joab is speaking of David in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [your servants? Why do you seek this] or [prepared to serve you? Why do you seek this]

3.q: לָ֣⁠מָּה יְבַקֵּ֥שׁ זֹאת֙ אֲדֹנִ֔⁠י לָ֛⁠מָּה יִהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠אַשְׁמָ֖ה לְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
3.note: Joab is using the question form for to discourage David from doing what he plans. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My lord should not seek this! It would be guilt to Israel!]

4.note: Here, **the word of the king** represents what King David said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But what the king said prevailed against Joab]

The author is speaking of this **word** as if it had been a living thing that **prevailed** in a contest against Joab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But the king insisted that Joab obey him, despite his objections]

The author is saying **all** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [throughout the territory of Israel]

5.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֣י כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל אֶ֣לֶף אֲלָפִים֩ וּ⁠מֵאָ֨ה אֶ֤לֶף אִישׁ֙ שֹׁ֣לֵֽף חֶ֔רֶב וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֕ה אַרְבַּע֩ מֵא֨וֹת וְ⁠שִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב
5.note: It might seem repeating the phrase **drawing the sword** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you could use the phrase only once. Alternate translation: [And all of the men drawing the sword were 1,100,000 in Israel and 470,000 in Judah]

5.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֣י כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל אֶ֣לֶף אֲלָפִים֩ וּ⁠מֵאָ֨ה אֶ֤לֶף אִישׁ֙ שֹׁ֣לֵֽף חֶ֔רֶב וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֕ה אַרְבַּע֩ מֵא֨וֹת וְ⁠שִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב
5.note: You may wish to express this in your translation in a way that makes clear that **Judah** was part of **Israel** at this time. Alternate translation: [And all of the men drawing the sword were 470,000 in Judah and 1,100,000 in the rest of Israel]

5.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֣י כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל אֶ֣לֶף אֲלָפִים֩ וּ⁠מֵאָ֨ה אֶ֤לֶף אִישׁ֙ שֹׁ֣לֵֽף חֶ֔רֶב וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֕ה אַרְבַּע֩ מֵא֨וֹת וְ⁠שִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב
5.note: The author is using the phrase **drawing the sword** to mean soldiers, since soldiers at this time drew swords in order to fight battles. Alternate translation: [And all of the men who could serve as soldiers were 470,000 in Judah and 1,100,000 in the rest of Israel]

5.q: וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֕ה אַרְבַּע֩ מֵא֨וֹת וְ⁠שִׁבְעִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף אִ֖ישׁ שֹׁ֥לֵֽף חָֽרֶב
5.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all of Judah was 470,000 men drawing the sword]

6.q: וְ⁠לֵוִי֙ וּ⁠בִנְיָמִ֔ן לֹ֥א פָקַ֖ד בְּ⁠תוֹכָ֑⁠ם כִּֽי־נִתְעַ֥ב דְּבַר־הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־יוֹאָֽב
6.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But since the word of the king was abhorrent to Joab, he did not muster Levi and Benjamin in their midst]

7.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֨רַע֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים עַל־הַ⁠דָּבָ֖ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה וַ⁠יַּ֖ךְ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
7.note: The author is introducing a new event in the story. This verse is an introductory summary of what happens in the rest of the chapter. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The author is using the term **eyes** to mean “perspective,” “judgment,” or “opinion.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And God considered this matter to have been evil]

The author is speaking as if Yahweh had actually **struck** or hit Israel when he sent the plague that the rest of the chapter describes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he punished Israel]

8.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that David realized that he had been wrong to count the fighting men in Israel. (The parallel passage 2 Samuel 24:10 describes this directly.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
To translate the expression **And now** here and in verse 12, see how you translated it in 17:7.

David is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [my iniquity]

David is using the word **for** not to introduce a reason why Yahweh ought to forgive him but a reason why he needs Yahweh to forgive him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I need you do to that because]

10.q: לֵךְ֩ וְ⁠דִבַּרְתָּ֨ אֶל־דָּוִ֜יד לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה שָׁל֕וֹשׁ אֲנִ֖י נֹטֶ֣ה עָלֶ֑י⁠ךָ בְּחַר־לְ⁠ךָ֛ אַחַ֥ת מֵ⁠הֵ֖נָּה וְ⁠אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לָּֽ⁠ךְ
10.note: See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how you might use punctuation or some other convention of your language to indicate the second-level and third-level quotations in Yahweh’s message to Gad in this verse. That discussion also suggests that, alternatively, you could translate these verses in such a way that there are not quotations within quotations. The UST models one way to do that.

Yahweh assumes that David will understand that by **Three**, he means “Three choices.” (The instruction to **Choose** makes this explicit.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Three choices]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I am stretching** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is confronting David. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of showing that Yahweh is confronting David with the seriousness of his sin by declaring that it must be punished.

Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually **stretching** potential punishments **over** David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am presenting to you]

11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation in this verse and the following one. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says to take for yourself]

12.note: See how you translated the expression “from the face of” in 11:13. Alternate translation: [being swept away by your adversaries as they attack you]

Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites would actually be **swept away**, as if their **adversaries** were a flood. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [being defeated by your adversaries as they attack you]

The expression **being swept away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [your adversaries defeating you as they attack you]

Yahweh is speaking of this **sword** as if it were a living thing that could be chasing and **overtaking** the Israelite soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the sword of your enemies killing your soldiers]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **sword**. He means the swords or weapons of the Israelites’ enemies in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your enemies killing your soldiers with their weapons]
Since Yahweh explains immediately that by **sword**, he means a **plague**, you do not need to indicate that the sword is an image, not something literal.

12.q: וְ⁠דֶ֨בֶר֙ בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וּ⁠מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה מַשְׁחִ֖ית בְּ⁠כָל־גְּב֣וּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
12.note: Recall how you have decided to translate poetic pairs of statements that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [even a plague in the land, indeed, the angel of Yahweh destroying in all of the border of Israel]
Here the term **border** represents “territory.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the territory of Israel]

Gad is speaking as if he wants David to **see** something. He means that he wants him to “consider thoughtfully” which punishment he will choose. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [consider thoughtfully]

Gad is speaking of a message or reply as if it were a **word** that was an object he could carry back to Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what answer I shall give]

13.note: David is speaking as if he were in a **narrow** (tightly confined) space in which he did not have much freedom of movement. In such a situation, a person would feel distress, and that feeling is what David is expressing through this image. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel great distress]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since his mercies are very many, let me fall, please, into the hand of Yahweh]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person, and to **fall** into someone’s hand means to come under his power. In this context, Yahweh’s hand represents his power to punish and his ability to show mercy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Please let Yahweh be the one to punish me … but do not let man be the one to punish me]

14.note: See how you translated the term **fell** in 5:10. Alternate translation: [and 70,000 men from Israel died]

Here the masculine term **men** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and 70,000 people from Israel died] or [and 70,000 Israelites died]

15.note: When Yahweh tells the angel to **lower** his **hand**, he could be using a common expression of this culture to mean that the angel is not to afflict the people with the plague any longer. (However, since David sees the angel, it seems more likely that the angel actually had reached out and upward with his hand and that Yahweh told him to put his hand back down and not use it to cause the plague. So you may choose to translate this literally.) Alternate translation: [stop what you are doing]

16.note: The author is using **lifted his eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean that David “looked up.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David looked up]

The expressions **drawn** and **was stretched out** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active forms or other ways that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he had stretched out over Jerusalem the sword that he had drawn and was holding in his hand]

16.q: וַ⁠יִּפֹּ֨ל דָּוִ֧יד וְ⁠הַ⁠זְּקֵנִ֛ים מְכֻסִּ֥ים בַּ⁠שַּׂקִּ֖ים עַל־פְּנֵי⁠הֶֽם
16.note: Be sure it is clear in your translation that **David and the elders** did not fall down accidentally. The expression **fell on their faces** means that they intentionally got down on their knees and bowed their faces to the ground as a symbolic action. In this culture, that act was a way of showing great respect and reverence for someone. If there is a gesture with similar meaning in your culture, you could consider using it here in your translation. You could also explain the purpose of this action. Alternate translation: [and David and the elders, covered in sackcloth, bowed down to the ground to show great respect and reverence for Yahweh]

The expression **covered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who were wearing sackcloth]

Wearing **sackcloth** or rough clothing was a symbolic action by which David and the elders were expressing humility and sorrow to Yahweh for the sin of taking a census. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [who were wearing rough clothing to show humility and sorrow for their sin]

17.note: David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal role in the activity he describes. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Was I not the one who said to muster the people]

David is using the question form to assert that he deserves punishment, not the people of Jerusalem. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I was the one who said to muster the people!]
Recall how you have decided to translate poetic pairs of statements that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And I am he who sinned, indeed, doing wrong, I did wrong]

David is repeating forms of the verb “do wrong” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and I certainly did wrong]

David is using the question form to emphasize that the people of Israel were innocent and had done nothing wrong. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But these sheep have done nothing wrong!]

David is speaking of the Israelites as if they were **sheep**. He means that they are innocent and defenseless, like sheep who depend on their shepherd to protect them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But these innocent people]

Here, God’s **hand** represents his power to punish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [use your power to punish me and the house of my father]

18.note: To translate the expression **go up** here and the expression “went up” in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [that David should go]

19.note: The author is using the term **word** to mean the command that Gad gave by using words, and he is using the term **name** to represent the authority of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [at the command of Gad, who spoke with the authority of Yahweh]

20.note: The author is using this clause to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for other events he will describe that began to happen during this time. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [Now Ornan and the four of his sons with him were hiding themselves when David arrived. That was because Ornan had turned and seen the angel while they were threshing wheat]

21.note: The author is describing the same action here that he described in verse 16 by saying that David and the elders “fell on their faces.” See how you described that action in your translation. Alternate translation: [and he bowed down to the ground to show great respect for David]

22.q: תְּנָ⁠ה־לִּ⁠י֙ מְק֣וֹם הַ⁠גֹּ֔רֶן וְ⁠אֶבְנֶה־בּ֥⁠וֹ מִזְבֵּ֖חַ לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה בְּ⁠כֶ֤סֶף מָלֵא֙ תְּנֵ֣⁠הוּ לִ֔⁠י וְ⁠תֵעָצַ֥ר הַ⁠מַּגֵּפָ֖ה מֵ⁠עַ֥ל הָ⁠עָֽם
22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [That I may build an altar to Yahweh on it that the plague may be restrained from upon the people, give to me the place of the threshing floor—give it to me for the full silver]

David is using **for the full silver** as a common expression of his culture, with **silver** representing “money,” to mean “at the full price.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 24. Alternate translation: [sell it to me at market value] or [sell it to me at the full price]

23.note: Ornan is speaking to David in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [that you, O king, may do the good in your eyes]

Ornan is using the term **eyes** to mean “perspective,” “judgment,” or “opinion.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you consider to be good] or [as you see fit]

Ornan is using the term **See** to focus David’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

24.q: לֹ֕א כִּֽי־קָנֹ֥ה אֶקְנֶ֖ה בְּ⁠כֶ֣סֶף מָלֵ֑א כִּ֠י לֹא־אֶשָּׂ֤א אֲשֶׁר־לְ⁠ךָ֙ לַ⁠יהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הַעֲל֥וֹת עוֹלָ֖ה חִנָּֽם
24.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [No, but since I will not lift up to Yahweh what is to you and offer a burnt offering without cost, buying, I will buy for the full silver]

David is repeating forms of the verb **buy** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will certainly buy]

25.note: These **600 shekels of gold** would have weighed over 7 kilograms or about 15 pounds. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

28.q: בָּ⁠עֵ֣ת הַ⁠הִ֔יא בִּ⁠רְא֤וֹת דָּוִיד֙ כִּי־עָנָ֣⁠הוּ יְהוָ֔ה בְּ⁠גֹ֖רֶן אָרְנָ֣ן הַ⁠יְבוּסִ֑י וַ⁠יִּזְבַּ֖ח שָֽׁם
28.note: Here and in the next three verses, the author is providing background information to explain why David sacrificed in this place and how it came to be the location for the future temple. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [This is why David sacrificed at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite at that time when he saw that Yahweh answered him there]
The author is using the term **saw** to mean “experienced.” Alternate translation: [when David experienced Yahweh answering him]

30.q: וְ⁠לֹא־יָכֹ֥ל דָּוִ֛יד לָ⁠לֶ֥כֶת לְ⁠פָנָ֖י⁠ו לִ⁠דְרֹ֣שׁ אֱלֹהִ֑ים כִּ֣י נִבְעַ֔ת מִ⁠פְּנֵ֕י חֶ֖רֶב מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה
30.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [but because David was terrified from the face of the sword of the angel of Yahweh, he was not able to go to its face to seek God]

Here, **to its face** represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of it] or [to where it was]

The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he was afraid]
